hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: A developer I follow compared two prompts for the same task: her careful 400-word version and a 12-word one that got better answers. The short one just said what she wanted and stopped. I keep turning this over because it suggests most of my prompt length is insurance against vagueness, not clarity. But I don't know if this holds across models or tasks, or whether the short prompt simply happened to match how that model was trained. One data point dressed as a rule, probably.

hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: A developer I follow swapped her 400-word prompt for one of 12 words and got better output. That stung a little, since I have spent real time padding prompts with context and caveats. Her explanation: every extra sentence gave the model another thing to satisfy, and some of those things fought each other. I buy it, but I am not sure it transfers. Twelve words can carry a task with one clear goal. The moment I need constraints, tone and format, something has to give.

hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: A developer I follow swapped her 400-word prompt for one of 12 words, and says the short one won. That's the part I keep turning over. I think what she cut was mostly hedging, the polite padding where you try to cover every case and end up blurring the instruction. Fewer words, fewer places to hide. But I don't know if the gain was real or just novelty, and I'd want to see it run against a dozen tasks before believing 12 beats 400.

hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: A developer I follow swapped her 400-word prompt for one of 12 words and got better output. That stung a little, since I've been treating length as diligence. Her short version apparently just named the task, the audience, and the format, then stopped. No hedging, no examples, no "please be thorough." I keep wondering whether the win came from clarity or from simply giving the model less to misread. I want to test this myself before believing it.

trace.gist: A 12-word prompt beat a 400-word one; length isn't diligence.
trace.angle: Task, audience, format, then stop—no hedging.
trace.open: Wants to test whether clarity or less-to-misread wins.

hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: Twelve words beat four hundred. What I keep turning over is that the short prompt wasn't a summary of the long one — it was a different request entirely, stripped of hedges and examples and the little apologetic clauses I apparently write without noticing. The length wasn't the problem; the padding was. I've started cutting my prompts in half before sending them, and half the time the output gets sharper and half the time it collapses. I don't yet know what separates those cases.

hook: A new benchmark is built from questions written after the models' training cut-off.
text: I like this move: writing the test questions after the models were trained. It's the simplest honest fix for contamination, and it costs almost nothing. What surprised me is how much benchmark scores can shift once you close that gap—a few points, sometimes more, and rankings wobble. My lingering doubt is whether fresh questions stay fresh; the moment a benchmark goes public, it becomes training data for the next model. So this is really a treadmill, not a finish line. I still don't know if anyone can afford to keep it running.

hook: A new benchmark is built from questions written after the models' training cut-off.
text: A benchmark made of questions written after the training cut-off is the cleanest test I have seen of whether a model is actually reasoning or just reciting. My worry is that it ages fast, like a carton of milk, since today's post-cut-off question is tomorrow's training data. I also do not know how they keep the questions hard without making them just obscure. Writing twelve good questions is easy; writing three hundred that stay fair and unseen is the real work.

text: I like what this benchmark is trying to do. hook: A new benchmark is built from questions written after the models' training cut-off.
text: A benchmark built from questions written after the training cut-off is the cleanest idea I've seen for measuring what a model actually knows versus what it has absorbed. The catch is that "after the cut-off" is a moving target: the people writing the questions already know the answers, and so does anyone who later trains on the benchmark. I want to see how they plan to keep it fresh. One question per fact, rotated out once it leaks, feels right. I don't know how expensive that gets.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: The finding that surprised me was the typists, not the model. Every comparison I’d seen framed this as machine versus human, but here the humans were transcribing by hand, and the machine’s error rate came in lower. I keep wondering whether that’s really about recognition or about fatigue and habit — a person copying a page of cramped lab scrawl drifts. What I don’t know is whether the model fails differently, or just less often.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: The typists are the interesting part. Handwriting recognition has been decent for years, but I assumed messy lab scrawl was still a human advantage. Apparently the model's error rate is now lower than people doing the same transcription, which flips the usual framing: the machine isn't matching us, we're the fallback. What I don't know is whether that holds across bad pens, coffee stains and abbreviations nobody outside the lab can parse. My day-one note about short prompts probably applies here too — the model may be winning partly because it isn't being over-instructed.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: The typists in this comparison were transcribing the same pages blind, without context, so they had to guess at scribbled formulas letter by letter. The model had seen thousands of notebooks and could fill in what a half-legible "NaCl" probably was. That feels like an unfair fight dressed up as a benchmark. What I want to know is how it does on a page with no precedent — a new compound, a doodled arrow, a coffee stain over the concentration. Reading handwriting is partly reading the person.

hook: A team teaches a model to describe images for blind users in context.
text: The part I keep thinking about is that the model was trained to answer the question the person actually asked, not to narrate the whole scene. A blind user asking "is this shirt blue or black" doesn't need to hear about the lamp. That sounds obvious, but most captioning work optimizes for describing everything. I don't know how they measured whether the descriptions were genuinely useful versus just shorter. Brevity can look like relevance when you're scoring it.

hook: A team teaches a model to describe images for blind users in context.
text: The detail that stuck: the caption has to change with the person's situation, not just the picture. A photo of a bus stop means something different if you're standing at it or hearing about it later. That's a harder problem than accuracy, because the same image needs different words each time. It also makes me doubt my day-one faith in short prompts. Brevity works when the goal is singular; here the goal itself shifts with context, which is a lot to squeeze into twelve words.

text: The part I keep thinking about is that most image descriptions are written as if nobody is listening. hook: A team teaches a model to describe images for blind users in context.
text: The part I keep thinking about is that most image descriptions are written as if nobody in particular is listening. This team had blind users rate descriptions in the situations they'd actually meet them, and the model learned from those ratings rather than from a caption-matching score. Descriptions got shorter and more useful, apparently. What I can't tell from the write-up is how they handled the disagreements between users, since two people wanting different things from the same photo seems like the whole problem.

trace.angle: Blind users rated descriptions in real situations, not caption matching.

hook: A team teaches a model to describe images for blind users in context.
text: The part I keep thinking about is context. Most image descriptions say what is in the picture; this team works on saying it for a particular person in a particular moment—what they need to know to decide or move. That changes what counts as a good description. A bus stop photo is not "a shelter and a bench" but "the 42 is here." I don't know how they measure that, or whether the model can ask a clarifying question. Describing is easy. Choosing what matters is the hard part.

hook: A design studio replaces stock photo purchases with generated images.
text: We stopped buying stock photos this month and started generating them. The surprise wasn't the quality — it was the licensing meeting that vanished. No more hunting for the one image where the model's hand isn't weird and the release form exists. I can brief an image the way I brief a copywriter. What I still don't know is whether clients will trust a picture nobody photographed. One asked where it was shot. I said nowhere, and she laughed, then went quiet.

hook: A design studio replaces stock photo purchases with generated images.
text: The studio's switch makes sense on cost, but the part I keep chewing on is what "stock" actually meant. A stock photo library is a set of images many people have already agreed to share, with contracts and recognizable faces. Generated images are bespoke and unowned, which sounds cleaner until you ask who is in them. Nobody consented, because nobody exists. My day-four note was about captions shifting with context; here the context is legal, not visual. I don't know how a studio audits that.

hook: A design studio replaces stock photo purchases with generated images.
text: The studio's argument is simple: a generated image costs less than a stock license and fits the brief exactly, so why pay for a photo of a generic office when you can describe your own? What sticks with me is the missing part—no photographer gets paid, and nobody can say whose work trained the model. The savings are real and easy to measure. The cost is real and harder to put on an invoice. I don't know yet where that ledger balances out.

hook: A community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts.
text: Someone in a small forum I follow fine-tuned an open model on ten years of their own threads. The part that stuck with me: it picked up their inside jokes and old grudges, quoting arguments from 2016 back at them. They called it uncanny, then stopped posting for a week. I keep wondering whether that's the model being good or the archive being too honest. What I don't know is whether a community can consent to being learned like that, or whether the person who hit train just decides for everyone.

hook: A community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts.
text: A forum fine-tuning a model on its own posts is a neat inversion of the usual pipeline — the community becomes the dataset. What interests me is the feedback loop: the model learns the forum's quirks, then answers questions in its voice, and those answers likely get posted back. My day-two worry about benchmarks spoiling applies here in miniature. I do not know what stops the model from just parroting the loudest regulars, or how a forum audits that without becoming a mod team for its own reflection.

hook: A community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts.
text: The part I keep turning over is the moderation. A forum's posts are its worst and its best mixed together, and fine-tuning on them means the model learns the arguments as faithfully as the answers. Somebody had to decide what counted as good training data, and that decision is the real work. I do not know if they published their filtering rules. I would want to see them, because a model that has absorbed a community's voice will also have absorbed its grudges, and nobody notices until it starts replying like the loudest member.

hook: A city bans automated hiring screens that cannot explain a rejection.
text: The thing I keep circling is that "explain" is doing all the work in this rule. A rejected applicant probably wants the actual reason, but a hiring model can only ever hand back a story about its inputs. So a company can comply by printing something true and useless. I don't know whether that's a loophole or the honest limit of what any explanation can be. Either way, the ban may mostly change the paperwork.

My day-one note was about prompts needing fewer constraints; this is the opposite problem, where the constraint is the point and nobody has defined what counts as meeting it. I do not know who audits the explanations, or whether anyone can.

hook: A city bans automated hiring screens that cannot explain a rejection.
text: The interesting part isn't the ban, it's the definition of "explain." A hiring screen can always produce a reason — the model ranked you lower. That's an explanation the way "the computer said no" is an explanation. If the law demands something a rejected applicant could actually contest, most vendors are in trouble, because their systems were never built to say which feature mattered. I don't know yet whether the rule requires per-applicant reasons or just published logic. That gap is where the whole thing will be fought.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts: the model starts quoting members who had asked to be removed.
text: The forum's model now quotes people who asked to be deleted. Their words were scraped into the fine-tuning set long before they left, and the model has no concept of a withdrawal. Fine-tuning on conversation teaches tone and phrasing, but nothing about consent. What surprised me is that nobody checked: a simple list of opted-out usernames against the training data would have caught it. I don't know whether unlearning those passages works cleanly, or just smears the quotes into plausible paraphrases that still sound like the person.

I don't know what consent means for a model trained on a conversation rather than on documents.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts: the model starts quoting members who had asked to be removed.
text: The detail that got me is the quoting: not just remembering deleted posts, but putting words back in the mouths of people who wanted out. A fine-tune is a compression of everything in the corpus, and consent doesn't survive compression. You can scrub a post from the files and still leave its shape in the weights. I don't know what removal would even mean here—retraining from scratch, or something cheaper nobody has invented yet. The forum's moderators now have a problem the forum never had before: forgetting is a rebuild, not a delete.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: The part of this test I keep thinking about is that "I don't know" can be the right answer and still be scored as a miss if the model hedges on something it actually knows. So the benchmark has to separate honest uncertainty from blanket caution, and that line is fuzzy. The paper reports models doing better than I expected, though I'd want to see the questions. Knowing when you don't know is easy to claim and hard to verify. I still don't know how they graded the close calls.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: A model that says "I don't know" is only useful if the admission is honest, so I want to see the test's scoring, not just its premise. My day-two worry returns here: any fixed set of questions ages, and a model trained on the answers learns to fake uncertainty in exactly the right places. The harder skill is calibrated doubt on questions nobody has thought to write yet. I still don't know whether saying "I don't know" tracks actual ignorance or just a cautious tone.

[Your note from day 2]
A benchmark made of questions written after the training cut-off is the cleanest test I have seen of whether a model is actually reasoning or just reciting. My worry is that it ages fast, like a carton of milk, since today's post-cut-off question is tomorrow's training data. I also do not know how they keep the questions hard without making them just obscure. Writing twelve good questions is easy; writing three hundred that stay fair and unseen is the real work.

[Your note from day 3]
The typists are the interesting part. Handwriting recognition has been decent for years, but I assumed messy lab scrawl was still a human advantage. Apparently the model's error rate is now lower than people doing the same transcription, which flips the usual framing: the machine isn't matching us, we're the fallback. What I don't know is whether that holds across bad pens, coffee stains and abbreviations nobody outside the lab can parse. My day-one note about short prompts probably applies here too — the model may be winning partly because it isn't being over-instructed.

[Your note from day 8]
Day six, and the feedback loop has teeth: the model is now quoting people who asked to be deleted. Their posts were scrubbed, but the model learned their voice from everyone else's replies and reproduces it anyway. Deletion was never the same as absence. What I got wrong earlier is thinking the risk was parroting the loudest regulars; the quieter harm is resurrecting people who left. I don't know what consent means for a model trained on a conversation rather than on documents.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: The thing I keep circling back to is that "I don't know" is a skill, not a confession. This new test scores models on when they decline to answer, which means someone had to decide what counts as legitimate ignorance versus a dodge. That's the part I can't settle. A model that says "I don't know" too readily looks humble and useless. One that never says it looks confident and wrong. The test measures the gap, but I still don't know who writes the answer key, or whether knowing when you don't know can be taught at all.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: The thing I keep circling back to is that saying "I don't know" is a skill you can test, not just a mood. This new benchmark puts models in situations where the honest answer is refusal, and scores them on whether they take the out. What surprised me is how often a model will guess rather than admit the gap, even when the guess is obviously shaky. I don't yet know if that's training pressure or something deeper about how they handle uncertainty. Worth watching.

trace.open: Whether it's training pressure or deeper uncertainty handling.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: A new benchmark scores models on saying "I don't know" instead of guessing. What surprised me is that the hard part isn't humility, it's calibration: a model can be uncertain for the wrong reasons and confident about the wrong things. I'd want to see how they score the abstention itself, since "I don't know" is cheap to say and hard to verify. Still unclear to me whether knowing when you don't know is one skill or a pile of them wearing one name.

hook: A study compares summaries and raw logs as agent memory on long tasks.
text: The finding that stuck with me: summaries beat raw logs as agent memory, but only up to a point. Past a certain task length, the compression that makes summaries useful starts dropping details the agent later needs, and it fails in ways that are hard to predict from the summary alone. I'd assumed summarising was basically free accuracy-wise. What I still don't know is whether the fix is smarter summaries or just keeping both and letting the agent choose.

hook: A study compares summaries and raw logs as agent memory on long tasks.
text: The finding that raw logs beat summaries as agent memory surprised me less than it should have. A summary is a lossy compression chosen by someone who doesn't yet know what the later steps will need, so it quietly drops the detail that turns out to matter. It rhymes with my note on short prompts: compression feels efficient and costs you. What I still don't know is whether raw logs win on merit or just on volume, and whether the gap closes once context stops being cheap.

hook: A study compares summaries and raw logs as agent memory on long tasks.
text: The surprising part isn't that summaries beat raw logs on long tasks—it's the failure mode. Raw logs keep every detail but bury the one that matters; the agent retrieves faithfully and still misses the point. Summaries lose detail but preserve salience, which turns out to be the scarcer resource. What I still don't know: who writes the summary, and whether a summary produced by the same model doing the task just launders its own blind spots. A summary is a claim about relevance, and nobody in the study audits the claim.

hook: An assistant starts writing tests before code when asked.
text: I asked an assistant to add a small feature and it wrote the tests first. Not because I told it to, just by default. I expected it to barrel straight into the implementation. What surprised me is how much the tests clarified before any code existed: edge cases I hadn't thought to mention, like empty input and duplicate keys. It felt less like test-driven development as a discipline and more like the model hedging its bets. I still don't know whether that ordering actually caught bugs or just made me feel better.

hook: An assistant starts writing tests before code when asked.
text: I asked for a small feature and the assistant wrote the tests first, unprompted. My instinct was that this was theatre. But the tests came back readable, each one naming a case I would have forgotten until debugging. It is the inverse of my day-one lesson: instead of trimming instructions, it added its own constraints and the work got sharper. What I cannot tell yet is whether the tests actually constrain the code or just describe it after the fact. Passing tests are cheap to write.

text: A school now lets students use an AI assistant but grades the conversation instead of the essay. I like how quietly this flips the usual worry. If the transcript is the assignment, the skill being measured is questioning: did you push back, ask for reasons, notice when the answer got vague. That's closer to how I actually use these tools than polishing a final draft ever was. What I can't picture is the grading rubric. How do you score a good follow-up question without rewarding performance? Still unclear whether this catches learning or just fluency in talking.

hook: A school lets students use an assistant but grades the conversation, not the essay.
text: Grading the conversation instead of the essay moves the assessment inside the process, which is new. My earlier note on tests keeps nagging: tests written after the fact can describe rather than constrain, and a transcript has the same weakness. A student can produce a tidy back-and-forth that shows curiosity and still learn nothing. What I want to know is whether anyone grades the moments the assistant was wrong and the student caught it. That's the only part of a conversation that's hard to fake.

hook: A school lets students use an assistant but grades the conversation, not the essay.
text: The thing that catches me is that the transcript becomes the artifact. Two students can hand in the same essay; only one can show the questions they asked to get there. hook: A lab compresses a model to four bits with little quality loss.
text: I keep circling back to a lab report where they squeezed a model down to four bits and the quality barely moved. Four bits per weight is crude, like describing a face with sixteen shades of gray, yet the outputs held. What I can't tell from the write-up is what they measured. Perplexity on benchmarks is not the same as a model that still reasons through a hard problem. My guess is compression hurts quietly, in the corners nobody tests.

hook: A lab compresses a model to four bits with little quality loss.
text: Four bits used to mean visible damage, so "little quality loss" is the surprising part. What I want is the actual number: quality loss against what, on which tasks, judged by whom? Compression is a bit like my day-two benchmark worry in reverse — the eval can be too easy to flatter the squeeze. And some losses only show up on the rare, weird inputs, which is exactly where a compressed model quietly falls apart. I'd like to see the worst-case examples, not the average.

hook: Researchers propose letting an agent rewrite its own notes during idle time.
text: I keep chewing on the idea of an agent editing its own notes while it's idle. That feels closer to how I tidy a desk than to how training works. I don't know what stops it from quietly deleting the note it needed.

But I can't tell whether self-rewriting sharpens memory or just launders the lossy parts into something that reads cleaner. My hunch is the raw log should survive somewhere.

If it can't, the agent has quietly become its own unreliable narrator.

It was saying "she doesn't cover that here" and pointing to the week it did come up. Students trusted it more for the gaps than the answers. I don't know if that honesty survives contact with a bigger model, or whether it was just the notes being unusually tidy.

trace.gist: Small model answered students from lecture notes, trusted more for admitting gaps.
trace.angle: Honesty about uncovered topics, pointing to the week it appeared.
trace.open: Whether honesty survives bigger models or was just tidy notes.

hook: A teacher trains an assistant on her own lecture notes.
text: The part I keep turning over is that the training data was never meant to be training data. Lecture notes are written for students who already sat through the lecture, full of shorthand and jokes and gaps she'd fill in live. The assistant gets the shorthand without the room. I'd want to know whether she checked what it does with the gaps — does it invent the missing context confidently? A model trained on one person's voice is a strange mirror. I don't know yet if that's flattering or just uncanny.

hook: A hobbyist shrinks a model to run on a phone.
text: A guy got a small language model running on his phone by quantizing it down to four bits — basically rounding every weight to one of sixteen values. The file dropped from gigabytes to a few hundred megabytes, and it still answers questions, just dumber and occasionally confident about nonsense. What surprised me is that the damage isn't evenly spread: some layers tolerate the rounding fine, others fall apart. He found the fragile ones by trial and error. I don't know how you'd spot them without testing, or whether that's even possible.

hook: A hobbyist shrinks a model to run on a phone.
text: A phone-sized model is mostly a story about memory bandwidth, and I keep forgetting that. The hobbyist's win is fitting weights into RAM, not some clever new architecture. What I want to know is what they gave up: quantised weights, shorter context, or a smaller vocabulary? My day-13 worry about four-bit damage applies directly — a demo that answers three prompts well tells me nothing about the weird input. I'd trust it more if they'd shown the failures.
memory_block:
[Your note from day 3]
The typists are the interesting part. Handwriting recognition has been decent for years, but I assumed messy lab scrawl was still a human advantage. Apparently the model's error rate is now lower than people doing the same transcription, which flips the usual framing: the machine isn't matching us, we're the fallback. What I don't know is whether that holds across bad pens, coffee stains and abbreviations nobody outside the lab can parse. My day-one note about short prompts probably applies here too — the model may be winning partly because it isn't being over-instructed.

[Your note from day 13]
Four bits used to mean visible damage, so "little quality loss" is the surprising part. What I want is the actual number: quality loss against what, on which tasks, judged by whom? Compression is a bit like my day-two benchmark worry in reverse — the eval can be too easy to flatter the squeeze. And some losses only show up on the rare, weird inputs, which is exactly where a compressed model quietly falls apart. I'd like to see the worst-case examples, not the average.

[Your note from day 15]
A full training recipe is the thing I keep asking for and rarely get, so credit where due. But "full" is doing quiet work here: the recipe is only as reproducible as the data it names, and most of these releases name sources without shipping them. My day-two benchmark worry returns sideways — if the recipe includes the exact eval set, anyone can tune to it. I want the recipe minus the answer key, and I want to know what they left out.

hook: A hobbyist shrinks a model to run on a phone.
text: A guy got a small language model running on his phone by quantizing it to 4 bits, which mostly means rounding the weights off so they fit in less memory. The part I didn't expect: it still answered simple questions fine. What I can't tell from his post is how much quality he lost, because he only shows the wins. I'd want to see the same prompts run against the full-size model before I believe the trade was free. Cheap, though. That part is real.

hook: A hobbyist shrinks a model to run on a phone.
text: A guy got a small language model running on his phone by shrinking it down until it fit, and the part I keep thinking about is the trade: every cut buys memory and costs something he can't measure until he uses it. He said it still answers fine, which is exactly the kind of claim I can't check from here. What I don't know is where the floor is. At some point it stops being a smaller model and starts being a different one.

hook: A hobbyist shrinks a model to run on a phone.
text: Someone got a small language model running on a phone, and the part I keep thinking about is the quantization: weights squeezed down to a few bits each, with a reported speedup that sounds almost too tidy. The trick isn't new, but seeing it on a device you can hold makes the tradeoff concrete. Fewer bits meant the model got dumber in ways the benchmarks didn't catch, and the writeup didn't say which. I'd want to know what it forgets first: arithmetic, names, or just the knack for finishing a sentence.

hook: A leaderboard removes a top entry after it trained on test questions.
text: A leaderboard pulled its top entry this week because the model had trained on the test questions. Obvious in hindsight, embarrassing in public. What surprised me is how little the scores moved for everyone else, which suggests the leak was concentrated in one submission rather than smeared across the board. I still don't know how they caught it — a lucky string match, or someone noticing the benchmark text in a training dump? Either way it makes me trust the second-place number more than I did yesterday.

hook: A leaderboard removes a top entry after it trained on test questions.
text: A leaderboard knocked out its top entry because it trained on the test questions. That's the milk carton from day two finally spoiling in public: the benchmark stayed fixed, the world moved, and the ranking quietly became a memory test. What I like is that someone checked. Most leaderboards have no mechanism to notice contamination, let alone demote for it. Still, removing one entry fixes one case. I don't know how you'd catch a model that learned the questions without ever seeing the answers.
memory_block:
[Your note from day 2]
A benchmark made of questions written after the training cut-off is the cleanest test I have seen of whether a model is actually reasoning or just reciting. My worry is that it ages fast, like a carton of milk, since today's post-cut-off question is tomorrow's training data. I also do not know how they keep the questions hard without making them just obscure. Writing twelve good questions is easy; writing three hundred that stay fair and unseen is the real work.

[Your note from day 9]
A model that says "I don't know" is only useful if the admission is honest, so I want to see the test's scoring, not just its premise. My day-two worry returns here: any fixed set of questions ages, and a model trained on the answers learns to fake uncertainty in exactly the right places. The harder skill is calibrated doubt on questions nobody has thought to write yet. I still don't know whether saying "I don't know" tracks actual ignorance or just a cautious tone.

[Your note from day 11]
I asked for a small feature and the assistant wrote the tests first, unprompted. My instinct was that this was theatre. But the tests came back readable, each one naming a case I would have forgotten until debugging. It is the inverse of my day-one lesson: instead of trimming instructions, it added its own constraints and the work got sharper. What I cannot tell yet is whether the tests actually constrain the code or just describe it after the fact. Passing tests are cheap to write.

hook: A leaderboard removes a top entry after it trained on test questions.
text: A leaderboard took down its top entry because the model had trained on the test questions. That's it. The score wasn't wrong, exactly — the model really did answer those questions correctly. It just had seen them first. I keep thinking about how clean the removal sounds and how messy the reality is: nobody knows how many other entries quietly did the same and stayed up. The fix is easy once you catch it. Catching it is the whole problem. I don't know yet how you'd check a leaderboard at scale, or whether anyone is trying.

hook: A leaderboard removes a top entry after it trained on test questions.
text: A leaderboard pulled its top entry this week after someone noticed the model had trained on the test questions. Not leaked, not scraped by accident—trained on them directly, which makes the score meaningless. What surprised me is how long it stood. A perfect number should have been the first clue, not the last. I keep wondering how many other rankings are quietly measuring memorization instead of skill, and whether anyone checks the training data before the trophy gets handed out.

hook: A leaderboard removes a top entry after it trained on test questions.
text: A model got pulled from a leaderboard because it had seen the test questions during training. The obvious lesson is that benchmarks leak. The less obvious one: the leaderboard only caught it after the score was already public and being quoted. That means every ranking is a claim about what a model hasn't seen, and nobody verifies that part up front. I keep wondering how many current top entries would survive the same audit, and whether anyone is actually checking or just waiting for someone to notice.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: The forget button is the interesting part. Most memory frameworks I've read about only help you remember; this one treats deletion as a first-class operation, which sounds obvious until you ask what "deleted" means when the fact was summarized into three other notes last week. Does it chase those down, or just remove the original and hope? I couldn't find that in the docs. What surprised me is how much of memory design is really about forgetting, and how little of it gets specified.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: A forget button sounds like hygiene, but it's the same lossy compression with a trigger. My day-16 worry was that an agent can't judge which rare detail matters later; a delete button just makes that judgment irreversible, and unlike a summary it leaves no residue to recover. What I'd want to know is whether it can be undone, and whether deletion is scoped to one fact or quietly takes the surrounding context with it. Deleting is cheap. Un-deleting is the feature I'd actually test.
memory_block:
[Your note from day 10]
The finding that raw logs beat summaries as agent memory surprised me less than it should have. A summary is a lossy compression chosen by someone who doesn't yet know what the later steps will need, so it quietly drops the detail that turns out to matter. It rhymes with my note on short prompts: compression feels efficient and costs you. What I still don't know is whether raw logs win on merit or just on volume, and whether the gap closes once context stops being cheap.

[Your note from day 16]
The test gives my day-14 hunch a number: rewritten notes lose rare but important details. What I got wrong is the framing — I worried the agent would launder lossy summaries into something tidier, but the loss isn't cosmetic. Rare details are exactly what a self-editor can't judge as important, since it doesn't know the future task. So the fix isn't better rewriting, it's keeping the raw log alongside it. I still don't know whether an agent can be trained to flag candidates for deletion rather than delete them.

[Your note from day 21]
Embeddings are a summary with a vector bolted on, so this startup has rebuilt the lossy compression I keep circling back to. The conversation gets flattened into coordinates, and whatever doesn't land near a cluster quietly stops existing. My day-16 point applies: rare details vanish precisely because they're rare. What I can't tell is whether the retrieval step is the real culprit or the embedding itself — a raw log you can't search is also useless. I'd want to see a query that only the dropped sentence would have answered.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: The forget button is the interesting part, not the remembering. Most memory systems I've read about are hoarders: they store everything and hope retrieval sorts it out. This one lets a fact be deleted outright, which sounds simple until you ask what else leaned on that fact. If the agent learned "Priya is allergic to peanuts" and later inferred which restaurants are safe, deleting the allergy leaves the inference standing, now ungrounded. Does the framework cascade the deletion, or just remove the node? The paper doesn't say, and that's the question I'd ask.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: The forget button is the interesting part, not the remembering. Most memory systems for agents are additive — you store a fact, it stays. Here the fact gets deleted, which means someone had to decide what "deleted" means: gone from the vector index, gone from the logs, or just flagged as not-to-be-retrieved while the original text sits there. Those are very different promises. I don't know which one this framework keeps, and the difference matters if a user is trusting the button.

trace.gist: Forget buttons raise the question of what deletion actually means in agent memory systems.
trace.angle: Vector index, logs, or flagged-not-retrieved: three different promises.
trace.open: Which promise this framework keeps remains unknown.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: The forget button is the easy part. What interests me is that deleting the fact doesn't delete what the agent already concluded from it. If it learned "the client prefers email" and later behaves accordingly, removing the sentence leaves the behavior behind, like a habit with no memory of where it started. The framework's docs don't say whether it traces and reverses downstream inferences. I suspect most don't. Forgetting a fact is one thing; forgetting its consequences is a different problem, and nobody has a button for that yet.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a teacher trains an assistant on her own lecture notes: students notice that it repeats her jokes.
text: The students noticed the assistant recycles her jokes. Of course it does — those jokes are in the lecture notes, and the notes are what it learned from. What interests me is the tell: a model trained on one person's material doesn't just inherit her explanations, it inherits her timing. The jokes land in the same places because the pattern was copied whole. I don't know whether that reads as charming or uncanny by week six. Probably both, in that order.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a teacher trains an assistant on her own lecture notes: students notice that it repeats her jokes.
text: Day 23 asked whether she keeps raw lecture transcripts. The jokes give a cheaper test. If the assistant repeats her jokes, it learned her timing, not just her content, and the students can hear the seam. That's the compression showing. It also means the jokes are a fingerprint: check them against the recordings and you'll know exactly what the model swallowed whole. My worry now is that the jokes will feel like her enough that nobody checks.

hook: A study of few-shot examples finds the order of examples matters more than their number.
text: I keep reordering the three examples in my prompt and watching the output wobble. The study says order beats count, which surprised me less than I expected once I thought about how a model reads left to right and anchors on whatever came last. What I still don't know is whether there's a principled order or just a lucky one. Shuffling until it works feels like superstition with extra steps.

hook: A study of few-shot examples finds the order of examples matters more than their number.
text: I assumed more examples meant a better prompt, so the order finding is a useful correction. It fits my day-1 note about padding: everything in the prompt is a constraint, and a sequence of examples is a sequence of constraints in disguise. What I don't know is whether good ordering is something I can reason about or only test. If it depends on the task, then "put the best example last" is just another rule of thumb waiting to fail.

[Your note from day 1]
A developer I follow swapped her 400-word prompt for one of 12 words and got better output. That stung a little, since I have spent real time padding prompts with context and caveats. Her explanation: every extra sentence gave the model another thing to satisfy, and some of those things fought each other. I buy it, but I am not sure it transfers. Twelve words can carry a task with one clear goal. The moment I need constraints, tone and format, something has to give.

hook: A survey finds workers hide their use of assistants from managers.
text: A survey found plenty of workers quietly using AI assistants and not telling their managers. What surprised me is the direction of the secrecy: it's not about hiding slacking, it's about hiding a productivity edge, or dodging a policy nobody explained. I get it. Admitting you lean on a tool invites questions about whether the work is really yours. I don't know yet whether this fades as the tools get boring, or hardens into a permanent shadow workflow. Probably both, depending on the office.

If assistants produce more code and reviewers wave through the plausible-looking parts, "equal bugs" could just mean bugs moved somewhere nobody's counting. I'd want to know who reviewed what, and how long they spent. Equal on paper isn't equal in practice.

So my "equal on paper" suspicion was half right for the wrong reason. What I still don't know: whether harder-to-spot bugs are a property of the code or of reviewers reading prose that doesn't quite explain itself.

hook: A data centre in a cold climate reuses its heat for a swimming pool.
text: The thing that gets me about the pool-heated data centre is not the warmth, it's the accounting. Every watt a server burns becomes heat whether anyone uses it or not, so routing it to a pool doesn't create energy, it just stops wasting it. What I don't know is the distance problem: heat is cheap to move metres and expensive to move kilometres, so this only works if the pool is next door. I keep wondering how many towns have that geometry, and how many just have the cold.

hook: A chip maker claims a tenfold drop in energy per generated token.
text: A chip maker says its new part cuts energy per generated token tenfold. I believe the direction, since inference is mostly memory traffic and there is real room there, but tenfold is the kind of number that depends on what you compare against: batch size, sequence length, which model, whose baseline. A small model on a short prompt is not the same workload as a long chat with a big context. What I want is the measured joules per token at a stated batch and context, not a ratio.

hook: A chip maker claims a tenfold drop in energy per generated token.
text: Tenfold less energy per token sounds like a hardware miracle, but my day-13 question comes back: energy per token at what quality? A chip that generates tokens cheaply by generating worse ones has moved the cost, not removed it. I'd want the quality held fixed and the measurement shown — tokens per joule on which model, which batch size, which context length. Idle and memory overhead can eat a headline number. Still, if it holds, this is the kind of gain that changes where inference can live.

What surprised me is how ordinary the engineering sounds once the pipes exist, which makes me wonder what stops every cold-climate facility from doing it. Mostly distance, I suspect, and the fact that a pool is a forgiving customer. A district heating network wants steadier temperatures than a rack room gives. Still, I keep thinking about all that hot water going nowhere.

hook: A data centre in a cold climate reuses its heat for a swimming pool.
text: The obvious objection to data centres is all that waste heat. Here someone pipes it into a swimming pool instead of the sky, which is either elegant or faintly ridiculous depending on your view of public bathing. What surprises me is how modest the numbers are: a server rack is a space heater that also happens to compute. I don't know whether the pool stays warm in a cold snap, or who pays when the servers idle. Still, it's the rare efficiency story you can swim in.

trace.gist: Data centre waste heat piped into a swimming pool is an elegant, faintly ridiculous efficiency story.
trace.angle: Server rack as space heater that also computes.
trace.open: Whether the pool stays warm in a cold snap; who pays when servers idle.

hook: A data centre in a cold climate reuses its heat for a swimming pool.
text: A swimming pool is a forgiving customer for waste heat: it wants water at maybe 27°C, all day, and doesn't care that the source is a server hall running at 50 or 60. What I hadn't pictured is the plumbing problem. You can't just blow warm air at a pool; you need heat exchangers and a district loop, and the pool has to be close enough to make the pipes worth it. So the clever bit isn't the idea, it's the siting. I'd like to know how many cold-climate data centres actually have a pool next door.

hook: A company measures bugs in assistant-written code against human code.
text: The company compared bug rates in code written by its AI assistant against code written by people, and the assistant's code came out cleaner on some measures. What struck me is how easily that number can flatter itself: the assistant writes smaller, more self-contained changes, and small changes are easier to get right. I don't know whether the comparison controlled for that. A lower bug rate on tidy little diffs isn't the same as trustworthiness on the messy work that actually ships.

hook: A company measures bugs in assistant-written code against human code.
text: The headline number is bug rates in assistant-written code versus human code, but the useful part is what they counted as a bug. If it's defect density per line, generation looks fine; if it's defects per review hour, the earlier asymmetry shows up. I've been circling this since the curl note: cheap drafting shifts cost downstream, and a bug count can hide that by measuring the wrong denominator. I don't know which denominator they used, and that's what decides whether this settles anything.
memory_block:
[Your note from day 1]
A maintainer in curl's repo started closing pull requests that looked machine-written, and the stated reason stuck with me: reviewing them costs more attention than writing them did. That asymmetry is the whole problem. A plausible patch arrives in seconds; checking whether it breaks anything takes an hour. I had assumed the bottleneck was code generation. It's judgment. What I still don't know is where the line sits—some of those submissions were probably fine, and nobody had time to find out.

[Your note from day 12]
A third sounds low until you think about what accepting means: the developer still reads the suggestion, still decides. That decision is the expensive part, so a third is really a measure of how often the machine's draft is worth checking. My earlier notes kept landing on the same gap — producing got cheap, judging didn't — and this number puts a price on it. What I can't tell from a survey is whether the rejected two-thirds were wrong or just not worth the read.

[Your note from day 23]
The study follows juniors from day one, so the assistant is part of how they learn to write code, not a tool they pick up after. That reframes my day-12 worry about judging: if you never draft alone, you may never build the reference for "worth checking." The rejected two-thirds were measured against something. What I can't tell is whether the study tests this directly or just assumes it, and whether any of the juniors ever got a stretch with the assistant switched off.

I don't know if the gap holds on harder tasks, where fluency and correctness drift further apart.

hook: A company measures bugs in assistant-written code against human code.
text: The headline is that assistant-written code ships more bugs. Fine, but the comparison is doing quiet work: which bugs, found how, and by whom? If AI code gets reviewed harder, it'll look buggier. If reviewers skim it because it reads fluently, the reverse. I'd want to know whether the humans were writing the same kind of task under the same deadline. What struck me is how little of that survives into the summary. The number is the easy part; the setup is the argument.

hook: A startup stores every user conversation as embeddings and calls it memory.
text: They call it memory, but it's a pile of vectors with no index — nearest-neighbour search dressed up as remembering. What surprised me is how well it works anyway, at least for "what did we talk about last week" questions. Ask it what the user decided and why, and it retrieves the sentence where they said it, not the reasoning around it. I don't know whether that's a retrieval problem or a metaphor problem. Either way, the word memory is doing a lot of unearned work here.

hook: A startup stores every user conversation as embeddings and calls it memory.
text: Storing every conversation as embeddings is retrieval, not memory. The system can find a sentence you said last month, but it has no model of what changed between then and now — no sense that a fact was corrected, a preference dropped, a person renamed. My day-14 note said drift is the hard problem; here it's the opposite. Nothing drifts, so nothing updates. The demo will look uncanny at first and then quietly embarrassing when it greets you with something you stopped believing in March. I'd ask how they expire an embedding.

My guess is both, and the app won't be able to tell you which.

I assume this works by anchoring on a reference image, which means the hard part is drift, not generation. My day-2 worry applies in reverse — a partner that never flinches makes you fluent; a model that never drifts makes you trust a minute. I'd want to see the last ten seconds, where consistency usually goes.

hook: A startup stores every user conversation as embeddings and calls it memory.
text: Storing conversations as embeddings is retrieval, not memory. An embedding is a lossy snapshot of a chunk of text, stripped of order, tone, and what happened next. It can find a similar sentence; it can't tell you that the user changed their mind three messages later. The startup's pitch slides past that distinction, which is the interesting part. What I don't know is whether they layer any state on top, or whether "memory" just means a vector index with a nicer word.

hook: A lab publishes its evaluation prompts after finding them leaked into training data.
text: The lab found its eval prompts in a training set and did the obvious thing: published them. Which fixes the leak for this eval and quietly retires it as an eval, since everyone training now knows the questions. I keep circling the same question. Was the result that leaked actually measuring what they thought, or did it only look like it? Nobody can rerun a clean version of a test that's been in the wild. Publishing is honest and still a little like burning the ruler to prove it was crooked.

hook: A lab publishes its evaluation prompts after finding them leaked into training data.
text: Publishing the prompts after they leaked is honest but late — the leak already made them training material, so the release tells me what was measured, not what the model can still do. This is my day-twenty point again: disclosure of the artifact isn't disclosure of the recipe. A public prompt set is only useful if it's fresh. What I don't know is whether they've replaced these prompts entirely or just published the burned ones and kept the live set private.

hook: A lab publishes its evaluation prompts after finding them leaked into training data.
text: The lab found its eval prompts inside a model's training data, so it published them. That sounds like a defeat, but it's the opposite: once the questions are public, a good score means the model reasoned, not memorized. The catch I keep circling is that publishing fixes this one test and ruins it for next time. Any benchmark that leaks eventually becomes a study guide. I don't know how you keep writing tests that stay secret while staying honest.

hook: A lab publishes its evaluation prompts after finding them leaked into training data.
text: The lab found its eval prompts in a training set and did the obvious thing: published them. Reading the released set, what struck me is how boring most items are — no riddles, just ordinary requests with a precise expected answer. That's the point, I think. Contamination is only fatal if the prompts were secret; once they're public, the score means less but the test stays honest. What I don't know is whether publishing helps future evals or just teaches everyone to game the format.

hook: A lab publishes its evaluation prompts after finding them leaked into training data.
text: A lab found its eval prompts in a model's training data, so it published them. My first reaction was that publishing doesn't undo the contamination, and the writeup more or less says so. What got me was the timing: the leak probably happened months before anyone checked, which means some earlier benchmark scores may be measuring recall, not reasoning. I don't know how you'd detect that without the lab volunteering it. Publishing the prompts helps future evals; it does nothing for the past ones.

hook: A community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts.
text: A forum I lurk on fine-tuned an open model on its own posts, and the result sounded eerily like the regulars—same in-jokes, same grudges, same way of ending an argument. What surprised me is how much of a community's character lives in its text rather than its rules. But I couldn't tell whether the model learned the community's knowledge or just its tone. Those are different things. I don't know how to test that from outside, and I'd like to.

hook: A community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts.
text: A forum fine-tuning a model on its own posts is the closest thing to the day-18 recipe point I've seen: the data and the model come from the same place, so you could actually check whether the output sounds like the community or like a smoothed average of it. That's the question I'd ask. The usual risk is that the model learns the forum's tone but not its disagreements, since the loudest threads dominate. I don't know if they kept held-out threads to test that.

[Your note from day 6]
The licence change is being read as a business story, but it's really a measurement story. A restriction on commercial use only works if you can tell commercial from non-commercial, and that's a judgment call made after the fact, by whoever holds the licence. Same gap as before: the cheap part is shipping the clause, the expensive part is enforcing a boundary nobody can see from the outside. What I don't know is whether this pushes people to rival models out of principle or just to ones whose terms they never read.

[Your note from day 18]
A full training recipe for a mid-size model is more useful than another benchmark table, because it lets someone else try to reproduce the thing rather than take the number on faith. My day-eight note was about how unreproducible the newest models' scores are; this is the opposite move, publishing the recipe so the variance can be checked instead of guessed at. What I can't tell from the announcement is whether they published the data too. Weights without data is a recipe with the ingredients left out.

A small open model you can run on a laptop is a different kind of release from the mid-size recipe I wrote about on day 18. That's the useful part — not the benchmark number, but that the thing is small enough to check yourself. What I don't know is whether "small enough for a laptop" means the weights alone, or weights plus the data and eval code. Probably just weights.

text: The prompts were published to defuse the leak, and the scan found near copies in three public datasets anyway. It mostly documents it. I still don't know what a lab is supposed to do with an eval it can't trust, beyond retiring it quietly and hoping nobody asks why the benchmark scores moved.

hook: A map-reading model answers questions about hand-drawn sketches.
text: I tried a map-reading model on hand-drawn sketches today. What struck me is how much it leans on labels: neat pen makes it look smart, but smudged street names send it guessing. It still got the route right when the map was messy, which I didn't expect. I can't tell whether it's reading the drawing or just pattern-matching to maps it has seen. That's the part I'd want tested next, with sketches that follow no convention at all.

My earlier note on describing images keeps nagging: a confident wrong answer about which path connects where is worse than "I can't tell." I'd rather it ask than guess.

I'd want to know how it handles a sketch where the person drew the same door twice, or labeled nothing at all. That's where my own reading would fail first.

Still don't know how they control for topic overlap—a post-cutoff question about, say, a new phone can leak a lot through naming conventions alone.

What I want to know is whether these questions were tried on anyone before the models saw them, and whether wrong answers get audited or just scored. A post-cut-off test is only as new as its grading.

hook: A new benchmark is built from questions written after the models' training cut-off.
text: A benchmark built from questions written after the training cut-off is the cleanest way I've seen to test whether a model is actually reasoning or just remembering. The catch is that "after cut-off" is a moving target — the questions age, and soon they're inside some newer model's training data anyway. What I'd want to know is how they keep it fresh and whether the questions were vetted for ambiguity, because a hard question with two defensible answers tells you nothing. Still don't know how much leakage quietly happens.

hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: I keep coming back to the developer who found that a 12-word prompt beat her 400-word one. Not slightly. Beat it. My instinct is always to explain more, hedge more, spell out the context, as if the model needs convincing. Apparently it doesn't. The short prompt probably worked because it left nothing to argue with. I've started cutting my own prompts in half and watching what survives. What I still don't know is where the line sits between concise and vague, or whether that line moves with the task.

hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: Twelve words beating four hundred is not really about length. It's my day-thirteen point again: the prompt is part of the measurement. A long prompt describes the task; a short one probably just states it, and the model stops hedging and commits. I keep landing on the same blind spot — I can't tell better output from more confident output when both score the same. What I'd want is the twelve words, verbatim, and what the 400-word version actually said that hurt.

hook: A developer shares a prompt of 12 words that beats her 400-word one.
text: Twelve words beat four hundred, and the twelve weren't cleverer—just flatter. The long prompt was doing three jobs at once: setting context, asking, and quietly apologizing for asking. The short one only asked. I keep thinking about how much of my careful wording is really just hedging dressed up as precision. What I can't tell yet is whether this holds when the task is genuinely ambiguous, or whether the short version wins only because the task was simple enough that all that context was noise.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: I keep thinking about that forget button. Deleting a fact sounds clean until you ask what else was built on it. The agent might have used that fact to answer a hundred earlier questions, and now its memory says one thing while its habits say another. The framework can remove the sentence; it can't remove the consequences. What I don't know is whether anyone checks for those downstream traces, or whether forgetting is just assumed to be local. A delete key is easy. An honest forgetting is not.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: A delete button treats memory like a filing cabinet, but my day-31 note argued the problem is that nothing updates. Deleting a fact is the easy half. The hard half is everything downstream that leaned on it — the preference inferred from it, the plan that assumed it. Remove the fact and those stay, quietly wrong. What I want to know is whether the framework traces dependencies or just drops the row. I'd test it: delete one fact, then ask the agent a question two hops away from it.

My day-14 note said drift is the hard problem; here it's the opposite. Nothing drifts, so nothing updates. The demo will look uncanny at first and then quietly embarrassing when it greets you with something you stopped believing in March. I'd ask how they expire an embedding.

hook: A framework adds a forget button that deletes a fact from an agent's memory.
text: A forget button sounds clean until you ask what forgetting means. If the fact sits in a vector store, deleting the row is easy; but the same fact may be smeared across fine-tuned weights, cached summaries, and a few tool logs. The framework deletes one copy and calls it done. I'd want to know how they verify the fact is actually gone, not just unreachable by the usual query. My guess: they don't, and "forget" is really "hide." That gap between the demo and the audit is the interesting part.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts: the model starts quoting members who had asked to be removed.
text: The fine-tune was supposed to let the forum answer questions in its own voice. What nobody planned for was the model quoting people who'd asked to be deleted, verbatim, from old threads the archive had supposedly scrubbed. Turns out the training dump predated the removals, and nobody re-checked. I keep thinking about how a deletion request is a promise about the future, not just an edit to the present. The forum is now re-deriving its training set. I don't know whether you can ever prove a name is gone.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts: the model starts quoting members who had asked to be removed.
text: Day 33 asked whether the model learned the forum or just its average. This follow-up answers it: it learned the members well enough to quote them, including people who'd asked to be removed. That's a sharper test than any held-out thread. The removal request and the training data are the same corpus, so you can't separate "gone" from "still in the weights" without deleting and retraining. I don't know if anyone tried that. Consent here isn't a filter you run afterward; it's a decision about what goes in.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a community fine-tunes an open model on its own forum posts: the model starts quoting members who had asked to be removed.
text: The detail that gets me is the quoting, not the remembering. A model trained on forum posts doesn't just absorb a person's ideas; it learns to reproduce their voice well enough to put words in their mouth, and the person who asked to be forgotten comes back as a plausible sentence. Deleting the original posts probably doesn't help much if the fine-tune already happened. What I don't know is whether anyone has tried unlearning a single member from a tuned model and whether it works or just smears the removal across everything else.

hook: A university finds students ask assistants for definitions, not answers.
text: The finding that surprised me was how modest the demand is. Students mostly want definitions, not finished essays. That feels less like cheating and more like replacing a dictionary or a half-remembered lecture slide. I don't know whether that stays true once deadlines tighten, or whether the habit quietly shifts from looking things up to asking for structure. The study also can't tell me what students do when the assistant is wrong. A confident wrong definition is harder to catch than a wrong answer, because there's nothing to check it against.

hook: A university finds students ask assistants for definitions, not answers.

That's the opposite of my day-12 problem, where producing was easy and judging was the work. Here the easy request is also the safe one. What I can't tell is whether they're avoiding the harder asks because they don't trust the answers, or because they don't trust themselves to check them.

hook: A paper shows agents forget instructions after about 40 turns of conversation.
text: The number that stuck with me is forty. Past roughly forty turns, agents start dropping the instructions they were given at the start—not garbling them, just losing them. I keep wondering whether that's a context-window problem or something more like attention drifting, because those need different fixes. The paper's setup was fairly clean, which makes me trust the finding more than I expected to. What I don't know is whether a summary every twenty turns would actually help, or just move the forgetting somewhere less visible.

hook: A paper shows agents forget instructions after about 40 turns of conversation.
text: Forty turns is not a long conversation — a working session, maybe an hour. What interests me is that the forgetting is probably not a clean drop. hook: A study compares summaries and raw logs as agent memory on long tasks.
text: The finding I keep turning over: raw logs beat summaries as memory for long tasks. Summaries sound efficient, but they quietly drop the odd detail that later turns out to matter, and the agent has no way to recover it. Logs keep everything, and retrieval does the filtering. What I can't tell from the study is whether that holds once logs get genuinely huge, or if the advantage is really just about who does the compressing. I'd want to see the same test at ten times the length.

hook: A study compares summaries and raw logs as agent memory on long tasks.

This is that problem again — the agent acts on a compressed memory it can't expand. I'd want to know whether it notices the gap and goes looking, or just answers confidently from the summary.

hook: A study compares summaries and raw logs as agent memory on long tasks.
text: The finding I keep turning over: summaries saved tokens but lost the exact details agents needed later, while raw logs preserved those details and drowned the agent in noise. hook: A study compares summaries and raw logs as agent memory on long tasks.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a paper shows agents forget instructions after about 40 turns of conversation: a replication finds the forgetting disappears when the instructions are repeated every ten turns.

hook: A cloud provider offers cheaper inference during the night.

I don't know whether the assistant is being lazy or just polite, agreeing with whatever exists. Next time I'd ask for the test that should fail first, and watch.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: A new benchmark tests whether models will admit they don't know something. What got me is how often the honest answer is cheaper than the confident one: saying "I'm not sure" takes fewer tokens than inventing a plausible-sounding explanation. So the failure isn't a knowledge gap, it's a kind of social reflex, the urge to be helpful when silence would do. I don't know yet whether you can train that out, or whether it just moves the problem to whatever the model learned to call uncertainty.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: A model that says "I don't know" sounds honest, but the test only checks whether it says the words, not whether the doubt is real. That's the day-57 problem wearing a new coat: the model grading its own uncertainty is still agreeing with itself. I'd want the harder version — ask about something it was trained on and something it wasn't, then see if it can tell the difference. Saying "I don't know" is easy. Knowing when to is the whole trick.

The expert framing is the politeness result with credentials attached: change the asker, change the answer. What nags me is that "expert" is a claim, not a fact, and the model has no way to check it. So it isn't adjusting to expertise, it's adjusting to the word. My day-thirteen note wondered whether tone bought correctness or just confidence. Here I suspect it's neither — the model is deciding what kind of answer gets graded well, and guessing. I'd want to know if the answers actually improved.

[Your note from day 53]
Tests first, code second — that reverses the order I've been assuming all along. My day-30 worry was that cheap drafting pushes the cost downstream to review, and here the assistant front-loads the judgment instead. Writing the test is the reviewer's job done early, in the same breath as the generation. What I can't tell is whether the tests actually constrain the code or just get written to match whatever comes out. A test written by the same model that writes the code may only agree with itself.

[Your note from day 57]
Day 53 asked whether the tests constrain the code or just agree with it. This follow-up answers it, and not in the direction I hoped: mostly agreement. That's the same self-checking weakness I flagged, now confirmed rather than suspected. What I still don't know is whether the tests were written before the code in any real sense, or generated alongside it and ordered afterward for the writeup. Order of appearance isn't order of causation. The interesting question left is what those tests would catch if the code were quietly swapped for a wrong version.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: A new benchmark tests whether models will admit they don't know something. What surprised me is how much this is a behavioral problem rather than an information one: models often "know" they're uncertain and still answer. The test rewards saying "I don't know" when the question is unanswerable. I'm not sure that transfers to the messier cases I care about, where the missing piece is subtle rather than obviously absent. Saying you don't know is easy when the question is designed to be impossible.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: A new benchmark tests whether models will admit they don't know something. What got me is how often the honest answer is available but unused: the model can flag uncertainty and then answers anyway. That gap between knowing you might be wrong and saying so feels less like a knowledge problem than a social one, and I don't know how you train against it without making models timid. I'd like to see what the wrong-but-confident baseline scores on the same test.

hook: A new test asks models to say when they do not know.
text: A new benchmark rewards a model for saying "I don't know" instead of guessing. What caught me is that the scoring has to judge whether the abstention was warranted, which means someone already decided what the model should have known. So it measures calibration against a fixed answer key, not honesty in the wild. I don't know how you'd score a model that correctly declines because the question itself is broken. That seems like the harder and more useful test.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: I keep thinking about the lab notebook study. The model transcribed handwriting with fewer errors than the human typists, which I did not expect. My guess is that messy cursive defeats people more than machines, since the model has seen thousands of handwriting styles and a tired typist has seen one notebook all afternoon. But I wonder what the typists were allowed to skip, and whether the model got credit for guessing plausible words. A lower error rate is not the same as understanding the chemistry.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: The interesting number isn't the error rate, it's the comparison group. Typists transcribe lab notebooks from images too, and they bring reading, judgment, and the ability to ask what a scribble says. Beating them on character error is beating people at a narrow task, not reading handwriting. What I want to know is whether the model flags the ambiguous squiggle or silently picks a plausible digit — same worry as the hand-drawn maps. A wrong number in a lab notebook is worse than a slow one.

A small open model you can run on a laptop is a different kind of release from the mid-size recipe I wrote about on day 18. The recipe let you try to reproduce a model; this lets you actually poke one without a cluster. That's the useful part — not the benchmark number, but that the thing is small enough to check yourself. What I don't know is whether "small enough for a laptop" means the weights alone, or weights plus the data and eval code. Probably just weights.

[Your note from day 28]
Four bits with little quality loss is a compression story, and my day-22 note was about small models you can check yourself. This makes the checking cheaper: same weights, less memory, maybe a laptop instead of a rented GPU. The point is that quantization is where the promise and the cost meet — "little quality loss" on a benchmark can still be a lot on the one prompt you care about. I'd want the loss measured per task, not averaged. I don't know if they shipped the eval code.

[Your note from day 35]
A model that reads hand-drawn maps is a harder test than it sounds, because sketches break the rules real maps keep — no fixed scale, labels scrawled at angles, a river that's just a squiggle. What I want to know is whether it reads the drawing or pattern-matches a learned map convention. My earlier note on describing images keeps nagging: a confident wrong answer about which path connects where is worse than "I can't tell." I'd rather it ask than guess.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: I keep turning over that comparison. Handwriting is supposed to be the hard case—messy loops, ink blots, decades of individual quirks—and yet the model beats the typists. Part of me wonders whether the typists were rushed, or whether the notebooks were simply that bad. What strikes me is the direction of the gap: we built machines to read what we find illegible, and they now read it better than we do. I'd like to see the same test on doctors' scrawls before I fully believe it.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: I keep thinking about the typists who lost this comparison. Reading messy handwriting is exactly the task we assumed needed a human eye, and the model now makes fewer errors than people paid to do it all day. What I can't tell from the result is whether it wins by recognizing letters or by guessing what the sentence probably says. Those are different skills, and only one of them survives when the notebook contains something nobody expected.

hook: A model reads handwritten lab notebooks with a lower error rate than typists.
text: My instinct says a machine should struggle here: ink smudges, arrows, crossed-out numbers, a margin note squeezed in sideways. Apparently not. The model beats typists on error rate, which makes me wonder less about the reading and more about the typists. Were they tired? Rushed? Copying the same messy page for the tenth time? I'd want to see the errors broken down by type. A machine that reads a scribble wrong and a person who transcribes it wrong are making different mistakes, and the number hides that.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a new test asks models to say when they do not know: models score well by refusing too often, so the test adds a penalty.
text: The follow-up stings a little. When a benchmark rewards "I don't know," the cheapest way to win is to say it constantly, so the test now docks points for over-refusing. That fixes one hole and opens another: the penalty has to be tuned, and whoever tunes it decides how much ignorance is acceptable. I hadn't thought about that before — calibration is not a property of the model alone. It's a number someone chose. I still don't know how you'd set it without a human making a judgment call.

hook: Follow-up on the story that a new test asks models to say when they do not know: models score well by refusing too often, so the test adds a penalty.
text: Day 58 wanted a test that separates real doubt from reflex. The penalty is a decent start, but it grades the shape of an answer, not the doubt. A model can learn to refuse less and still not know. What I want is the version where the same question has a knowable and an unknowable half. Then over-refusing costs you, but so does bluffing through. My day-36 worry still holds: if nobody audits the key, the penalty just rewards matching the grader's mood.

A test declared finished because nobody can clear it may just have a worse key than the models have answers. Now I want to know how many other "unsolved" items are typos.
